name: Stalecheck — continuous vendor-master refresh for mid-market AP teams
one_liner: For the AP manager or financial controller at a 50-500 person company with 200-2,000 suppliers in NetSuite, Xero or QuickBooks, Stalecheck re-verifies every supplier record against live public evidence each month — still trading, name/registration changed, insolvency filed, website dead, duplicate of another vendor — and hands back a ranked worklist of the 20 records that actually need a human.
problem: Mid-market AP teams carry a vendor master that nobody re-checks after onboarding. Suppliers get acquired, rebrand, dissolve, go into administration, or change registration numbers; records duplicate under slightly different names; dormant vendors sit active for years as an open payment path. Today the fix is either (a) nothing, until a payment bounces, an auditor flags it, or a fraudster exploits a dormant record, or (b) a one-off "vendor master cleanse" consultancy project priced by the hour (MDM work commonly quoted $50-300/hr per a 2026 roundup; treat as an estimate), or (c) an enterprise fraud platform. CDQ-attributed figures cited in industry write-ups put business-partner record decay around 21%/year and duplicates around 16%; an Infosys BPM client sample found ~25% of customer/vendor records inactive or redundant. The enterprise answers (Trustpair, Eftsure, nsKnox) are sales-led with no published self-serve price — Eftsure's own pricing page says pricing depends on annual spend and new-vendor volume; one nsKnox page lists $8,000/yr for 100 validations/month — and they are built around bank-account verification at payment time, not a standing monthly audit of the existing file for a team with 400 suppliers.
target_customer: AP manager, financial controller or finance ops lead at a 50-500 employee company (services, e-commerce, light manufacturing, agencies, multi-site hospitality) running NetSuite, Xero, QuickBooks Online or Sage, with 200-2,000 active suppliers. Buyer is the controller or CFO; budget line is "finance systems / audit prep". Secondary buyer: outsourced accounting and CFO-services firms who would run it across their client base.
why_now: Web-grounded decision APIs shipped this month at a price that makes per-record monthly re-verification economically trivial: Parallel's Decisions API launched 27 Oct 2026 at $0.001 per request covering up to 100 questions, with citations and 200ms-1s latency and 5,000 free requests. Re-checking 1,000 suppliers against ~8 questions each costs roughly $1 per pass (estimate from published pricing). Liquid's d1-2B decision models (LFM Open License, Hugging Face) give a self-hostable fallback for customers who refuse to send supplier lists to a third party. Before these, "ask a structured, cited yes/no about 1,000 small companies every month" meant a scraping pipeline plus an LLM bill, which is exactly why only enterprise-priced vendors did it.
comparables: Trustpair (trustpair.com) — bank-account ownership verification + vendor-master monitoring, 190 countries, ERP integrations; quote-only, enterprise-sized, G2 reviewers report slow checks in some countries and inconclusive results; gap: no self-serve tier, built around payment-time verification. Eftsure (eftsure.com) — same category with a US$1M guarantee; its own pricing page states price depends on annual expenditure and monthly onboarding, no published figures; gap: sales-led, enterprise AP. nsKnox/PaymentKnox (nsknox.net) — publishes an SMB tier at $8,000/yr for 100 validations/month; gap: priced per validation event, not a standing file audit, and still 10x a mid-market controller's discretionary spend. Coupa (coupa.com) — has continuous supplier-risk monitoring and duplicate flagging, but as part of a full source-to-contract suite with unpublished buyer pricing; gap: far more suite than a 400-supplier team needs. Creditsafe / Company Watch / FilingPing (filingping.co.uk) — registry-change alerts, strong on UK Companies House events, free or cheap; gap: they alert on a watchlist you build, they do not read your ERP vendor file, dedupe it, or tell you which records to retire. Clay/ZoomInfo-style enrichment — aimed at sales prospecting, not the AP ledger, and does not produce an audit trail. The specific unserved workflow: "connect my accounting system, audit the supplier file I already have, every month, and give me a short worklist with evidence I can paste into an audit folder."
market_note: Estimates, clearly labelled. There is proven willingness to pay adjacent to this: nsKnox publishes $8,000-12,000/yr SMB tiers for 100 validations/month; Trustpair and Eftsure are quote-only enterprise contracts; Eftsure's revenue reportedly tripled on AI-driven scam fear (AFR, Nov 2025). That pricing leaves an obvious hole beneath it. A plausible first wedge: $200-600/month for up to 1,000 supplier records, sold to controllers who would never clear an enterprise procurement cycle. If 2,000 mid-market finance teams in UK/US/AU paid $400/month that is ~$10M ARR — a wedge, not a category. The bigger prize is becoming the standing "supplier file health" layer that outsourced accounting firms resell across hundreds of client ledgers. Gross margin is very high: data cost is ~$1-5 per full pass per customer.
risks: Accuracy on long-tail small suppliers — a web-grounded model confidently mislabelling a live vendor as dissolved is the fastest way to lose a finance buyer, and the mitigation (confidence thresholds + evidence links + never auto-acting) caps how much work you actually remove. Frequency risk — if this is genuinely an annual audit-prep chore, the subscription collapses into a cheap one-off and the business is a consultancy. Incumbent squeeze — Trustpair, Eftsure or Coupa can add a "file audit" view to accounts they already hold, and they already own the bank-verification trust story; the defence is to stay below their price floor and sell through accounting firms rather than direct enterprise procurement.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That controllers treat a stale vendor file as a *scheduled* job worth a subscription, rather than something they only touch at year-end audit — if it is annual, this is a $500 one-off report, not SaaS. 2) That web-grounded decisions are accurate enough on small, obscure suppliers (a two-person plumbing contractor, a foreign freelancer) that the worklist is not 80% false positives; one bad "this supplier is dissolved" on a live vendor destroys trust. 3) That read-only ERP access is obtainable without a security review that costs more than the contract — i.e. that CSV export plus a Xero/QBO OAuth app is enough for the first 10 customers.
first_customers: (a) Outsourced accounting / fractional CFO firms — Bench-style and local practices on r/Accounting, the Xero and QuickBooks ProAdvisor partner directories, and UK ICAEW practice listings; one firm gives access to 10-30 client ledgers at once. (b) Controllers in 100-300 person e-commerce and agency businesses found via the NetSuite and Xero user groups on LinkedIn, r/Accounting and r/AccountsPayable, and the IOFM/AFP community forums. (c) Internal audit and finance leads at multi-site hospitality and construction firms, who already pay for one-off vendor cleanses. Concretely: run the free audit on 10 real supplier exports sourced from these communities before writing any ERP integration.
validation_test: This week: post in r/Accounting, r/AccountsPayable and two Xero/NetSuite LinkedIn groups offering a free "supplier file health report" — they email a CSV of supplier name + address + registration number (no bank details), and within 48h get back a PDF listing dissolved/renamed/dormant/duplicate records with a citation per finding. Run it manually with Parallel Decisions plus Companies House/state registry lookups. Pass: 10+ exports submitted within 7 days, and at least 4 recipients reply confirming findings they did not know about; hard pass if 2+ say "send me a quote" unprompted. Fail: fewer than 5 exports, or recipients confirm findings but say "interesting, we'd check this once a year".
build_plan: Narrowest first version, no ERP integration: a CSV in, PDF + CSV out audit. (1) Upload supplier CSV (name, address, country, registration number if present, last payment date). (2) Normalise and dedupe locally — fuzzy name + address matching flags candidate duplicates, no AI needed. (3) For each record, one batched Parallel Decisions call with ~8 typed questions: is this entity still trading; has it changed legal name; is there an insolvency/administration/dissolution filing; is the registered address still valid; is the website live; is it the same entity as <duplicate candidate>; each returning a probability plus citations. (4) Score and rank: only surface records above a confidence threshold, always with the evidence link, never auto-change anything. (5) Output a one-page PDF ("412 suppliers checked, 19 need attention, 7 likely duplicates, 3 dissolved") plus a CSV worklist with an evidence URL per row, designed to be dropped into an audit folder. (6) Charge $299 for the first report, then $299/month for a monthly re-run with a diff ("new since last month"). Cut for v1: ERP write-back, bank-account verification (regulated, slow, where the incumbents are strong), sanctions screening, non-English registries beyond UK/US/AU, any auto-remediation.
reasoning:
Two tracks, two different problems and buyers: Stalecheck sells a recurring audit workflow to AP managers and controllers inside their accounting ledger; Deadlist is a free, open-source paste-a-list toy for builders, writers and analysts on X. They share only the background observation that records about companies go stale — not an audience, a workflow or a product.

Venture pick. The Parallel Decisions API launch named "refresh stale banking records" as a use case; the interesting move is not to build that for developers (crowded) but to follow it into a back office. Research showed the vendor-verification category is real and monetised (Trustpair, Eftsure, nsKnox, Coupa) but uniformly sales-led: Eftsure publishes no price and scales by annual expenditure, nsKnox's own SMB page lists $8,000/yr for 100 validations a month, Coupa's buyer pricing is unpublished. All of them are organised around verifying a bank account at onboarding or payment time. Nobody I found sells a cheap, standing monthly audit of the supplier file a 300-person company already has, delivered to a controller who cannot run an enterprise procurement cycle. That is the gap I scored, not the category. Timing is genuinely new: at $0.001 per batched request with citations, re-verifying 1,000 suppliers costs about a dollar a pass, and d1-2B under the LFM Open License gives a self-host answer for data-sensitive buyers. I scored gap and market_pull at 7 rather than 8 because I confirmed the incumbents' pricing opacity but did not talk to a single controller — the frequency assumption (monthly subscription vs annual audit chore) is unvalidated and is the thing the free-report test must settle. Pain is expressed: teams already buy one-off cleanses and enterprise fraud tools.

Build pick. Deadlist is the taste-file shape — one paste, one surprising scoreboard, free, open source, no signup. Every dependency is checked: published price, published rate limit (600/min), published free tier, and a documented requirement to keep the key server-side, which the build plan respects. Usefulness scored only 5 and that is honest — this is closer to a one-time curiosity than a weekly habit, which is the single strongest reason it fails; the narrow way around it is the saved-list diff, deliberately held back from v1 so the weekend ship stays a weekend. Freshness and buildability carry it.

Candidates dropped as repeats of the library: anything built on the skill-diet bookmark (a skill-audit or skill-token tool) collides directly with SkillProof and SkillPeek — same agent-developer audience, same inspect-a-SKILL.md workflow. The DigitalOcean Action Gateway bookmark points straight at Doublecheck, Ledger and Driftwatch — same agent-reliability buyer and the same intercept-the-tool-call wedge — so I dropped it despite being a good post. RWE-Bench would have produced an eval/benchmark product, which is EvalSeed and AgentGauntlet territory.

Both ideas clear 6, so both are filed; the venture takes the top-level slot on a 7.2 vs 7.2 tie only because the build's score rests on a weaker usefulness leg. Both get verdict "watch", not dig_deeper: in each case the decisive question (does a controller pay monthly / does anyone return a second time) is untested, and tonight's research checked pricing and prior art, not demand.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Stalecheck — continuous vendor-master refresh for mid-market AP teams (KEPT, lead). Real paid incumbents prove the pain, but all are quote-only and payment-time focused; the standing monthly file audit for a 400-supplier controller is unserved and newly cheap to deliver.
2. Grant/tender eligibility pre-screening for nonprofits and SMEs using web-grounded decisions (DROPPED). Instrumentl at $299-999/mo already does profile matching and owns the buyer; the "true eligibility check" sliver is legally fragile — a wrong pass/fail is worse than no answer — and the buyer is budget-poor.
3. Supplier/counterparty adverse-news monitoring for procurement (DROPPED). Owlin, RapidRatings, Coupa and Creditsafe already serve this buyer with this workflow at enterprise scale; no narrow unserved slice surfaced in search, and it is the same "monitor an entity" shape as the lead without the ledger wedge.
4. Cloud-exit / AWS-to-bare-metal migration as a productised service, from the Hetzner bookmark (DROPPED). A real market exists but it is already competed as consultancy (WZ-IT from €1,990, CloudExit Pro on 20% of savings) and it is a services business, not an agent-edge software venture — poor fit for this builder's profile.
5. Anything derived from skill-diet, Action Gateway or RWE-Bench (DROPPED AS REPEATS). Collide with SkillProof/SkillPeek, Doublecheck/Ledger/Driftwatch, and EvalSeed/AgentGauntlet respectively — same buyers, same core workflows.

BUILD
1. Deadlist — paste any list of companies, get ALIVE/DEAD/ACQUIRED/RENAMED with citations (KEPT, runner-up slot). Perfect one-input/one-output shape, every dependency price-checked, and the closest prior art is a vendor's own closed demo.
2. Genie 4 world-model toy, e.g. turn a photo into a walkable world (DROPPED). Most striking bookmark of the night by engagement, but access is waitlisted via Project Genie for Google AI Ultra subscribers with Gemini API availability unconfirmed — cannot ship this weekend.
3. On-device LFM3-Audio or LFM3-VL browser toy, e.g. a private local meeting-notes or video-describer (DROPPED). Weights are genuinely available on Hugging Face under the LFM Open License, but a day disappears into quantisation and runtime plumbing before anything is visible on screen, and the wow is "it runs locally" rather than the output itself.
4. Skill token-bloat visualiser from the skill-diet post (DROPPED). Repeat of SkillPeek's audience and workflow, and skill-diet itself plus several community skills already do the optimisation.
5. CSV row-enrichment playground ("ask a question about every row") (DROPPED). Directly the crowded Clay/Oppora/GPT-for-Sheets space with good free options already; Deadlist is the same technology aimed at one sharper, more shareable question.
research_notes:
Reading pot (3/3 used): summarised the Parallel Decisions API launch (confirmed $0.001/request for up to 100 batched questions, 5,000 free, 200ms-1s latency, citations, and what Jev/decision models are), RWE-Bench (20 tasks, 11 models, deterministic engineering verifiers — interesting but eval territory already in the library), and the LFM3 family (open weights on Hugging Face under the LFM Open License, GGUF/ONNX/MLX builds, d1-2B typed decisions self-hostable). I cannot see images or video, so the Genie 4, Cursor Annotate, Wonder and macOS-dock posts were judged on text plus search only.

Venture pot (11/12 used): checked DigitalOcean Action Gateway in detail (policy allow/ask/deny, $0.10 per 1,000 invocations) and used it to rule the whole agent-governance direction out as a library repeat. Then worked the back-office angle: searched insurance-broker AI (found Covera in YC, buyer already being served), procurement/supplier monitoring (Owlin, RapidRatings — enterprise, served), CRM data decay (Clay/ZoomInfo — wrong buyer, sales not finance), then narrowed to AP and vendor master. Summaries on Trustpair/nsKnox/Creditsafe and on Eftsure/Trustpair/nsKnox self-serve pricing produced the decisive finding: no published self-serve tier anywhere, nsKnox's own SMB page at $8,000/yr for 100 validations/month, Eftsure pricing scaled to annual expenditure. A further summary on Tipalti/Coupa/Basware/Apex established that continuous monitoring exists mainly inside full procurement suites with unpublished buyer pricing, and that scheduled audits of the *existing* NetSuite/Xero file are the unverified gap. Statistics summary surfaced CDQ-attributed ~21% annual record decay and ~16% duplicates plus an Infosys BPM sample at ~25% inactive/redundant — all labelled as directional, not industry benchmarks. A grant-eligibility summary and a UK Companies House monitoring search killed two alternative candidates (Instrumentl owns the grant buyer; FilingPing/Company Watch already do free registry alerts but never touch your ledger). This research is what moved the venture from a generic "web-grounded monitoring" idea to the specific CSV-in/worklist-out wedge priced under the incumbents.

Build pot (7/7 used): confirmed Genie 4 shipped 27 Oct 2026 but is waitlisted via Project Genie for AI Ultra subscribers with Gemini API access unconfirmed — that killed the highest-engagement build candidate. Searched skill token-optimisation tooling and found community skills already doing it, confirming the repeat. Searched fact-checking apps, one-click company due-diligence tools, CSV enrichment tools and "still in business" checkers: enrichment is crowded and paid, but no free, open, paste-a-list status checker surfaced. A final summary confirmed the Decisions API needs a server-side key, has a 600 req/min limit and a 5,000-request free tier, and that Parallel's own demos (including a YC company status checker) exist but are not verifiably open source — which set Deadlist's differentiation (arbitrary pasted lists, open source, explicit UNSURE state) and forced the serverless-route architecture into the build plan.
prototype_summary: An interactive Stalecheck prototype where a controller clicks "Run monthly check" and a wall of 14 identical "Active" vendor-master rows resolves into six specific, evidenced, actionable findings with retire/keep controls.
